author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Diagnose slow PS2 gameplay when menus remain full speed
summary: Compare menu, lightweight gameplay, and one heavy scene with matched counters to identify whether the workload scales with game logic, geometry, effects, or resolution instead of using menu speed as proof of compatibility.
heroAlt: Final Fantasy X gameplay scene used to illustrate a workload that differs from lightweight menus

blocks.text: A menu often draws few objects, runs limited simulation, and can reach full speed on hardware that struggles in gameplay. Select three checkpoints: the menu, a quiet playable area, and the heaviest reproducible scene. Record emulation speed, frame time, audio, and available EE, VU, GS, draw, or GPU timing indicators at each point without restarting into different profiles.
Do not claim a title is fully compatible from its menu or opening logo. Those paths may exercise only a fraction of the CPU, VU, graphics, storage, and synchronization workload.

items: A save in a quiet playable area and another before a known heavy scene.
The same regional image, renderer, driver, resolution, and power mode.
A warm cache state established before the measured route.
Counters or a synchronized recording visible at all three checkpoints.
Stable device temperature and no background downloads.

blocks.text: Measure how cost appears as gameplay complexity rises

items: 1. Record thirty seconds in the menu after cache warm-up.
2. Load the quiet area and follow a fixed camera path for one minute.
3. Load the heavy scene and repeat its deterministic combat or traversal route.
4. Compare emulation speed and subsystem timing across all three points.
5. Lower only internal resolution and rerun the heavy scene as a GPU-sensitivity probe.
6. Restore resolution and compare one alternate stable renderer if the scene is graphics-sensitive.
7. If resolution has little effect, inspect CPU, VU, draw-call, and game-logic timing instead.
8. Save a per-scene table and choose the daily profile from the heaviest valid checkpoint.

blocks.text: The ladder shows where cost enters. A quiet area that is already slow points to a broad CPU or compatibility problem; a resolution-sensitive heavy scene points toward host graphics load; a scene that stays slow at native resolution may be dominated by emulated logic or synchronization. Menu results remain useful only as the lightest reference.
A useful classification explains the measured progression from menu to gameplay and repeats on demand.

items: All checkpoints use one unchanged baseline profile.
The heavy route is reproducible rather than random.
Resolution sensitivity is tested as a single variable.
Audio and emulation speed agree with numeric timing.
The selected profile survives the heavy scene twice.
Different savestates load different hacks: cold-boot normal saves.
The heavy run begins after thermal decline: normalize temperature.
Resolution and blending change together: split the variables.
Only average FPS is recorded: include speed and frame-time behavior.

blocks.text: Restore internal resolution and renderer to the last verified values, remove temporary counters, and cold-boot the heavy save once. Store the checkpoint table with the per-game profile so later changes are judged against actual gameplay rather than menu speed.
A title can have several unrelated heavy scenes

One boss may be CPU-heavy while another area is GPU-heavy or storage-sensitive. The procedure classifies the tested checkpoint; extend the ladder when a later scene violates the accepted performance budget.
